pages.title: Process
pages.content:
One batch at Taruki Distillery takes nine days and makes 420 bottles. It moves through six stages on a 300-litre copper pot still named Ottilie: Botanicals, Steep, Still, Cut, Rest and Bottle.

Head distiller Mira Okafor makes every cut by taste at the spout, and every bottle is filled, corked and labelled by hand.

Book a tour

pages.title: Botanicals
pages.content:
Nine botanicals go into every batch: juniper, Larchmere lemon peel, bitter orange, coriander, angelica, orris, bay, pink pepper and sea fennel. The peel comes from the Hillside Grove above the harbour.

See the bottles

pages.title: Tours
pages.content:
Tours run Wednesday to Sunday at 11:30, 14:00 and 16:00, for up to 12 guests aged 18 and over. The Still-Room Tour with a three-gin tasting is €32 (60 minutes); the Tour with a Cut Tasting at the spout, with a G&T, is €48 (90 minutes).

The Botanical Blending Workshop (3 hours, 50 cl bottle to take home) is €115, and a private group tour for up to 10 guests is €390.

Book a visit

pages.title: Shop
pages.content:
Larchmere Citrus Peel Gin, 70 cl, 43%: €44. Navy Cut Gin, 50 cl, 57%: €49. Both are bottled by hand at the distillery, 420 bottles to a batch.

pages.title: About
pages.content:
Taruki Distillery was founded in 2016 at 14 Quarry Lane in Larchmere by Mira Okafor, around a single 300-litre copper pot still named Ottilie. We make small batches of 420 bottles over nine days, and we cut every run by taste.

Read the journal

pages.content: Mira Okafor, founder and head distiller. Tomasz Wren, still operator. Inès Dubreuil, botanical forager. Kenji Halvorsen, tasting room lead. Ana Lucía Ferro, tour guide. Ruth Abernathy, bottling and labels. Samir Haddad, citrus grower at the Hillside Grove.

posts.title: Inside batch 112: a week at the still
posts.excerpt: A day-by-day record of steeping, steam and cutting our current run.
posts.content:
Batch 112 started on a Tuesday, when Inès brought the first trays of dried peel in from the drying room. By Wednesday the botanicals were steeping in Ottilie, and the smell in the still room was juniper first, then lemon.

Day four is the cut. Mira stands at the spout with a small glass and tastes the run every few minutes, setting aside the harsh foreshots and tails and keeping only the heart. It is slow work, and it is the reason a batch is only 420 bottles.

After the cut the spirit rests for several days before it is brought down with local water and bottled by hand on day nine.

posts.title: Why Ottilie runs slowly
posts.excerpt: How gentle copper temperatures keep the subtle citrus notes.
posts.content:
Ottilie is a 300-litre copper pot still, and we run her gently. Low steam keeps the delicate oils in the juniper, coriander and citrus peel from scorching, and the long contact with the copper dome cleans the vapour.

A faster run would be cheaper. It would also taste flatter. So we keep the nine-day cycle and let the still take its time.

posts.title: Peel from the Hillside Grove
posts.excerpt: Partnering with Samir Haddad for fresh orchard fruit.
posts.content:
In 2019 Mira began buying peel from Samir Haddad, who tends lemon and bitter orange trees on the hill above Larchmere. The fruit is hand-harvested, and the peel is pared thin the same day.

It changed the gin. The lemon is brighter, the bitter orange rounder, and the sea air of the hillside is in the glass.
